Published · Co-author

Experimental and numerical investigation of flexural energy absorption in octopus suction-cup-inspired FDM-printed sandwich structures

S. Baidya, S. Ahmed, T. A. Fahim, H. R. Paul, M. A. Hasib, A. M. Billah, A. K. Debnath. Materials Today Communications 57, 116421 (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.mtcomm.2026.116421 Read paper

1 / 3

Sandwich structure and suction-cup core designs (Fig. 2) · Source: this paper

The question

Nature-inspired cores such as honeycombs are well studied, but marine-life geometries are not. Can the curved cavity of an octopus sucker be used to tune the trade-off between stiffness and energy absorption in a 3D-printed sandwich panel under bending?

Our approach

We designed three suction-cup cores (AV1–AV3) with growing cavity area, printed them as single-piece PLA+ sandwich panels by FDM, characterized the material in tension, ran three-point bending tests, and validated the results with ANSYS finite-element models before a parametric study on leg thickness.

What we found

A larger cavity lowers stiffness and peak load, but makes failure progressive instead of abrupt. The AV3 core absorbed the most energy, showing that cavity geometry alone can shift the panel from stiff-and-brittle to energy-absorbing.

Bio-inspired CAD FDM printing (PLA+) Tensile test 3-point bending FEA validation Parametric study
6.45 Jenergy absorbed by the AV3 core
+167%energy absorption vs. AV1
~1063 Npeak load of the stiffest core (AV1)
0.175 J/gspecific energy absorption (AV3)
Key findings
  • Increasing cavity area steadily reduces stiffness and peak load.
  • AV1 is strongest but fails suddenly; AV3 deforms progressively and absorbs the most energy.
  • FEA matched the measured peak forces and energy, and was used to explore four leg-thickness variants.
02
Published · Co-author

Performance Enhancement of Sisal Fiber Epoxy Composites Using TiO₂ and CuO Fillers

S. Ahmed, A. A. Ahsun, T. A. Fahim, A. K. Debnath, M. A. Hasib. Polymer Composites (2026). DOI: 10.1002/pc.71546 Read paper

1 / 3

SEM images of CuO and TiO₂ filler particles (Fig. 1) · Source: this paper

The question

Natural fibers like sisal are cheap and sustainable, but they absorb water and bond poorly to epoxy. CuO and TiO₂ had never been compared side by side in the same sisal/epoxy system: which filler helps more, and at what loading?

Our approach

We made unidirectional sisal/epoxy laminates by hand lay-up with 1, 1.5 and 2 wt% CuO or TiO₂ dispersed by ultrasonic sonication, then ran tensile, flexural, short-beam shear and water-absorption tests to ASTM standards, backed by SEM, XRD and FTIR.

What we found

Both fillers improved the composite. Flexural strength rose by more than half at 2 wt%, interlaminar shear strength increased, and TiO₂ cut water uptake sharply, because the particles filled voids and improved fiber–matrix bonding.

Filler sonication Hand lay-up Tensile & flexural Short-beam shear Water absorption SEM · XRD · FTIR
+54.8%flexural strength with 2% TiO₂
+51.3%flexural strength with 2% CuO
9.01 MPashort-beam shear strength (1% TiO₂)
−47.5%water absorption with TiO₂
Key findings
  • 2% CuO gave the highest tensile and interlaminar shear strength.
  • 2% TiO₂ gave the largest flexural gain and the lowest moisture uptake.
  • SEM showed better fiber–matrix bonding; XRD and FTIR confirmed physical interfacial interaction.
03
Published · Co-author

Experimental and Numerical Study on Fly Ash-Reinforced Core of 3D Printed PETG/Wood-PLA Honeycomb Sandwich Composites

J. A. Chowdhury, T. A. Fahim, S. Baidya, M. S. Islam, M. A. Hasib. Arabian Journal for Science and Engineering (2026). DOI: 10.1007/s13369-026-11182-5 Read paper

1 / 3

Printed honeycomb sandwich specimens (Fig. 2) · Source: this paper

The question

3D-printed honeycomb cores are light but weak in compression and conduct heat. Can filling the cells with a sustainable fly ash geopolymer make them stronger and better insulating, and what does it cost in bending?

Our approach

We printed hexagonal honeycomb cores in PETG and Wood-PLA between 1.6 mm face plates, filled them with fly ash geopolymer, and tested compression (ASTM C365), flexure (ASTM C393) and thermal properties by the transient plane source method, supported by FEA and SEM.

What we found

The geopolymer filling roughly doubled the compressive strength of PETG cores and lowered thermal conductivity, but reduced bending strength because the filler bonds poorly to the thermoplastic. PETG with geopolymer gave the best insulation.

Honeycomb CAD FDM printing Geopolymer infill Compression & flexure Thermal (TPS) FEA & SEM
~2×compressive strength of filled PETG cores
−20%flexural strength, PETG
−54%flexural strength, Wood-PLA
2printed polymers compared
Key findings
  • Geopolymer infill strongly improves compressive behaviour of both cores.
  • Weak polymer–geopolymer adhesion reduces bending strength, confirmed by FEA and SEM.
  • Filled cores insulate better: lower conductivity and diffusivity, higher specific heat.

Published · Co-author

Fiber-reinforced fly ash geopolymers: Effect of fiber type and curing duration on mechanical strength, weight loss, and microstructure

N. Rahim, T. A. Fahim, S. Uddin, A. K. Debnath, M. A. Hasib, D. Mondal. Structural Concrete (2026). DOI: 10.1002/suco.70469 Read paper

1 / 1

Sample preparation process (Fig. 2) · Source: this paper

The question

Kevlar and carbon–Kevlar hybrids are rarely used in geopolymers, and little is known about how curing duration affects their bond with the matrix. When does each fiber reach its best strength?

Our approach

We cast fly ash geopolymers with 1% carbon, 1% Kevlar and 1% hybrid fibers using a 10 M NaOH / sodium silicate activator, cured them for 3, 7, 14 and 28 days, and measured compressive and flexural strength, weight loss and microstructure by SEM.

What we found

Kevlar gave the best strength, peaking after 7 days. Single fibers peaked early and then declined, the hybrid peaked at 14 days, and plain geopolymer kept gaining strength to 28 days. Kevlar also showed the best fiber–matrix bonding.

Mix design Fiber addition Curing 3–28 days Compression & flexure Weight loss SEM
21.39 MPacompressive strength, 1% Kevlar (7 days)
4.27 MPaflexural strength, 1% Kevlar (7 days)
18.22 MPahybrid peak at 14 days
7.35%weight loss of the hybrid (plain: 8.31%)
Key findings
  • Carbon and Kevlar composites peak at 7 days, then lose strength, likely from fiber degradation or interfacial microcracking.
  • The carbon–Kevlar hybrid peaks later, at 14 days.
  • SEM shows the strongest fiber–matrix bond with Kevlar.

Published · First author · Review

Recent advances in fiber-reinforced geopolymer composites: A systematic review of optimization strategies

T. A. Fahim, R. A. Emon, A. A. Kafi, P. D. Nath, A. K. Debnath, M. A. Hasib. Next Research 2, 100955 (2025). DOI: 10.1016/j.nexres.2025.100955 Read paper

1 / 3

Types of geopolymer composites (Fig. 1) · Source: this paper

The question

Fiber-reinforced geopolymers could replace carbon-heavy Portland cement, but results on fiber type, dosage and curing are scattered across the literature. What does the evidence say about the best combinations?

My approach

I led a systematic review built around three research questions, collecting experimental data from major publishers on natural fibers (coir, cotton, bamboo) and synthetic fibers (steel, carbon, glass, Kevlar, basalt, amorphous metallic), and comparing curing conditions, elevated-temperature behaviour and techno-economics.

What I found

Fiber percentage is decisive, with a clear optimum for each fiber type. Curing temperature and time strongly affect final properties, with strength improving for longer curing up to 28 days, and geopolymers offer cost and environmental advantages over conventional materials.

Research questions Literature search Data extraction Fiber & curing analysis Techno-economics Recommendations
3research questions framing the review
9+natural and synthetic fiber types compared
28 dayscuring window over which strength keeps improving
80–90%lower CO₂ than Portland cement, per the literature
Key findings
  • Each fiber type has its own optimum content for compressive and flexural strength.
  • Controlled curing temperature and time are as important as fiber choice.
  • Applications include fire-resistant, high-strength construction and infrastructure.

Conference · First author

Numerical Comparison of Natural Convection Heat Transfer in Air- and Water-Filled Enclosures

T. A. Fahim, M. M. Rahman, I. H. Sharar. Proc. ICMIEE 2024, SciEn Conference Series: Engineering 3, 337–342 (2025). DOI: 10.38032/scse.2025.3.95 Read paper

1 / 3

C-shaped enclosure schematic (Fig. 1) · Source: this paper

The question

Air and water had been compared in rectangular cavities, but not in C-shaped enclosures. How do the enclosure shape and the fluid together control buoyancy-driven heat transfer?

My approach

I simulated 2-D laminar natural convection in ANSYS Fluent with the Boussinesq approximation, for aspect ratios of 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7 and Rayleigh numbers from 10⁴ to 10⁶, using a 120,000-element mesh validated against classic square-cavity benchmarks.

What I found

Secondary eddies forming under the cold rib boost mixing and heat transfer. Water generally transfers more heat thanks to its higher conductivity and heat capacity, but in some configurations the eddy pattern in air becomes especially effective.

Geometry Mesh (120k cells) Validation Fluent simulations Streamlines & isotherms Nusselt comparison
10⁴–10⁶Rayleigh number range
3aspect ratios studied
120kmesh elements after independence test
8.855validation Nu at Ra = 10⁶ (benchmark 8.799)
Key findings
  • More secondary eddies appear under the cold rib as the aspect ratio grows.
  • Water-filled enclosures mostly give higher heat transfer than air-filled ones.
  • Enclosure shape and fluid properties must be chosen together for thermal management.
03
Conference · Corresponding author

Numerical Comparison of Laminar Natural Convection Heat Transfer in C-shaped and U-shaped Enclosures

I. H. Sharar, M. M. Rahman, T. A. Fahim. Proc. ICMIEE 2024, SciEn Conference Series: Engineering 3, 181–186 (2025). DOI: 10.38032/scse.2025.3.46 Read paper

1 / 3

C- and U-shaped enclosure geometry (Fig. 2) · Source: this paper

The question

Few studies compare C-shaped and U-shaped enclosures at low Rayleigh numbers. How does the aspect ratio change heat transfer in each shape?

Our approach

We modelled both enclosures filled with air in ANSYS Fluent (2-D, laminar, Boussinesq), with a hot outer wall, cold inner rib and adiabatic connecting walls, across three aspect ratios and Rayleigh numbers from 10⁴ to 10⁶.

What we found

The Nusselt number rises with Rayleigh number in both shapes, but at different rates. Higher Rayleigh numbers create more eddies, which steepen temperature gradients and give the highest heat transfer at Ra = 10⁶.

C & U geometry Mesh Validation Fluent simulations Streamlines & isotherms Nusselt comparison
2enclosure shapes compared
3aspect ratios (0.3, 0.5, 0.7)
10⁴–10⁶Rayleigh number range
120kmesh elements
Key findings
  • Nusselt number increases with Rayleigh number for both shapes.
  • Eddy formation drives the change in heat transfer, most clearly at certain aspect ratios.
  • C- and U-shapes respond at different rates as Ra increases.

Elevated Temperature Behavior of Bagasse and Human Hair Fiber-Reinforced Fly Ash Geopolymer Composites

M. H. A. Mahbub, M. A. Hasib, T. A. Fahim, A. K. Debnath, M. S. Rabbi, M. A. Islam. Engineering Reports 7(12), e70571 (2025). DOI: 10.1002/eng2.70571 Read paper

1 / 3

Fiber preparation (Fig. 1) · Source: this paper

The question

Can low-cost waste fibers, sugarcane bagasse and human hair, keep fly ash geopolymers strong enough for use in hot environments?

Our approach

We reinforced fly ash geopolymer with 1, 1.5 and 2 wt% of each chopped fiber, exposed the samples to 200–800 °C, and measured compressive and flexural strength, with SEM to study the fiber–matrix interface.

What we found

Strength falls with temperature, but human hair retains it much better than bagasse thanks to stronger bonding and lower porosity. Composites with up to 1.5% fiber stay usable for moderate-temperature applications between 200 and 600 °C.

Fiber preparation Mix & cast Heat 200–800 °C Compression & flexure SEM analysis
13.62 MPahuman-hair composite at 800 °C (from 24.45)
7.12 MPabagasse composite at 800 °C (from 25.87)
1.5%fiber content with sufficient integrity
200–600 °Crecommended service window
Key findings
  • Human hair outperforms bagasse in strength retention across all temperatures.
  • SEM shows stronger bonding and less porosity with human hair.
  • Both are viable, sustainable alternatives to synthetic reinforcement.

Published · Co-author

Physical and Thermomechanical Performance of Kevlar and Carbon–Kevlar-Reinforced Geopolymer Composites at Elevated Temperatures

A. K. Debnath, M. A. Hasib, R. A. Emon, A. A. Kafi, T. A. Fahim, M. S. Rabbi. Journal of Engineering 2424227 (2025). DOI: 10.1155/je/2424227 Read paper

1 / 3

Crack formation and porosity after heating (Fig. 2) · Source: this paper

The question

Kevlar and carbon–Kevlar hybrids are strong and light, but their behaviour inside geopolymers at up to 800 °C had not been studied systematically. How do they compare?

Our approach

We made fly ash geopolymers with 1, 1.5 and 2% Kevlar or hybrid fiber, heated them to 200–800 °C, and measured compressive and flexural strength, visual damage and thermal conductivity, with SEM of the fracture surfaces.

What we found

Kevlar at 1% gave the best strength at 200 °C. Hybrid composites strengthened with more fiber but became brittle at 800 °C. Both lost more than half their thermal conductivity at 800 °C, which is useful for insulation.

Mix design Fiber dosing Heat 200–800 °C Mechanical tests Thermal conductivity SEM

10.02 MPaflexural strength, 1% Kevlar at 200 °C
−54.6%thermal conductivity drop, Kevlar at 800 °C
−59.2%thermal conductivity drop, hybrid at 800 °C
Key findings
  • Kevlar bonds better to the matrix and reduces porosity.
  • Hybrid composites are stronger at higher fiber content but more brittle at 800 °C.
  • Strength partly recovers at 800 °C, likely from microstructural densification.

Effect of Elevated Temperatures on the Mechanical and Thermal Performance of Fly Ash Geopolymers with Varying Carbon Fiber Content

A. K. Debnath, M. A. Hasib, R. A. Emon, A. A. Kafi, S. Roy, S. Uddin, T. A. Fahim, N. Rahim. IUT-ICCET 2024 · IUT Journal of Engineering and Technology, special issue 608–626 (June 2025). Journal page

1 / 3

Fabrication flowchart (Fig. 2) · Source: this paper

The question

Carbon fiber improves geopolymers, but how thermal load affects their mechanical and fracture behaviour had not been examined. Are they suitable as fire-resistant building materials?

Our approach

We compared unreinforced geopolymer with 1, 1.5 and 2% carbon fiber composites after heating to 200, 400, 600 and 800 °C, measuring compressive and flexural strength, mass loss and thermal conductivity, with SEM to follow crack growth.

What we found

Carbon fiber raised flexural strength and kept it high even at 800 °C, while thermal conductivity stayed low, making these composites promising fire-resistant, thermally stable construction materials.
